How to Fix the Internet

如何修好互联网

原文全文译文

[A] We have to fix the internet. After 40 years, it has begun to corrode, both itself and us. It is still a marvelous and miraculous invention, but now there are bugs in the foundation, bats in the belfry, and trolls in the basement.

[B] I do not mean this to be one of those technophobic rants insulting the internet for rewiring our brains to give us the nervous attention span of Donald Trump on Twitter or pontificating about how we have to log off and smell the flowers. Those worries about new technologies have existed ever since Plato was concerned that the technology of writing would threaten memorization and oratory. I love the internet and all of its digital offshoots. What I feel sad for is its decline.

[C] There is a bug in its original design that at first seemed like a feature but has gradually, and now rapidly, been exploited by hackers and trolls and malevolent actors: Its packets are encoded with the address of their destination but not of their authentic origin. With a circuit-switched network, you can track or trace back the origins of the information, but that’s not true with the packet-switched design of the internet.

[D] Compounding this was the architecture that Tim Berners-Lee and the inventors of the early browsers created for the World Wide Web. It brilliantly allowed the whole of the earth’s computers to be webbed together and navigated through hyperlinks. But the links were one-way. You knew where the links took you. But if you had a webpage or piece of content, you didn’t exactly know who was linking to you or coming to use your content.

[E] All of that protected the potential for anonymity. You could make comments anonymously. Go to a webpage anonymously. Consume content anonymously. With a little effort, send email anonymously. And if you figured out a way to get into someone’s servers or databases, you could do it anonymously.

[F] For years, the benefits of anonymity on the net outweighed its drawbacks. People felt more free to express themselves, which was especially valuable if they were holding different opinions or hiding a personal secret. This was celebrated in the famous 1993 New Yorker cartoon, “On the Internet, nobody knows you’re a dog.”

[G] Now the problem is nobody can tell if you’re a troll. Or a hacker. Or a bot. Or a Macedonian teenager publishing a story that the Pope has supported Trump. This has poisoned civil discourse, enabled hacking, permitted cyberbullying, and made email a risk.

[H] The lack of secure identification and authentication inherent in the internet’s genetic code had also prevented easy transactions, obstructed financial inclusion, destroyed the business models of content creators, unleashed the overflow of spam, and forced us to use passwords and two-factor authentication schemes that would have confused Houdini. The trillions being spent and the IQ points of computer science talent being allocated to tackle security issues make it a drag, rather than a spur, to productivity in some sectors.

[I] In Plato’s Republic, we learn the tale of the Ring of Gyges. Put it on, and you’re invisible and anonymous. The question that Plato asks is whether those who put on the ring will be civil and moral. He thinks not. The internet has proven him correct. The web is no longer a place of community, no longer a marketplace. Every day more sites are eliminating comments sections.

[J] If we could start from scratch, here’s what I think we would do: Create a system that enables content producers to negotiate with aggregators and search engines to get a royalty whenever their content is used, like ASCAP has negotiated for public performances and radio airings of its members’ works. Embed a simple digital wallet and currency for quick and easy small payments for songs, blogs, articles, and whatever other digital content is for sale. Encode emails with an authenticated return or originating address. Enforce critical properties and security at the lowest levels of the system possible, such as in the hardware or in the programming language, instead of leaving it to programmers to incorporate security into every line of code they write. Build chips and machines that update the notion of an internet packet. For those who want, their packets could be encoded or tagged with metadata that describe what they contain and give the rules for how it can be used.

[K] Most internet engineers think that these reforms are possible, from Vint Cerf, the original TCP/IP coauthor, to Milo Medin of Google, to Howard Shrobe, the director of cybersecurity at MIT. “We don’t need to live in cyber hell,” Shrobe has argued. Implementing them is less a matter of technology than of cost and social will. Some people, understandably, will resist any reduction of anonymity, which they sometimes label privacy.

[L] So the best approach, I think, would be to try to create a voluntary system, for those who want to use it, to have verified identification and authentication. People would not be forced to use such a system. If they wanted to communicate and surf anonymously, they could. But those of us who choose, at times, not to be anonymous and not to deal with people who are anonymous should have that right as well. That’s the way it works in the real world.

[M] The benefits would be many. Easy and secure ways to deal with your finances and medical records. Small payment systems that could reward valued content rather than the current incentive to concentrate on clickbait for advertising. Less hacking, spamming, cyberbullying, trolling, and spewing of anonymous hate. And the possibility of a more civil discourse.

全文译文

[A] 我们得修好互联网。四十年过去了，互联网已经开始侵蚀自身，也在侵蚀我们。它依然是一项了不起的发明，但如今就像一栋房子，地基里有虫子，钟楼里有蝙蝠，地下室里还藏着捣乱的人。

[B] 我无意像那些惧怕技术的人一样，长篇大论地骂互联网改变了我们的大脑，让我们像在推特上的唐纳德·特朗普一样，注意力短暂而容易分散。我也无意摆出说教的姿态，劝大家下线去感受生活中的美好。对新技术的担忧由来已久，柏拉图就曾担心书写技术会威胁记忆和演讲的能力。我喜爱互联网以及由它衍生的一切数字事物。我为它的衰落感到惋惜。

[C] 互联网的原始设计有一处缺陷，起初看起来像是一项功能，却逐渐被黑客、网络喷子和其他心怀恶意的人利用，如今这种利用愈演愈烈。数据包编码中有目的地地址，却没有真实的来源地址。在电路交换网络中，你可以追踪信息的来源，而互联网采用的分组交换设计做不到这一点。

[D] 蒂姆·伯纳斯-李和早期浏览器的发明者为万维网搭建的架构，又加深了这个问题。这一架构巧妙地把全球的计算机连成网络，让人们可以通过超链接浏览。但链接是单向的。你知道点击链接会去哪里，可如果你有网页或发布了内容，就很难确切知道谁链接到了你，或者谁来使用你的内容。

[E] 这一切保留了匿名的可能性。你可以匿名发表评论、访问网页、浏览内容。稍费些工夫，也可以匿名发送邮件。如果你找到进入别人服务器或数据库的办法，也可以匿名操作。

[F] 多年来，网络匿名的好处大于弊端。人们觉得表达自己更自由了，尤其是在持有不同意见或想保守个人秘密时。1993 年《纽约客》那幅著名漫画就赞扬了这一点：“在互联网上，没人知道你是一条狗。”

[G] 现在的问题是，没人能判断你是不是网络喷子、黑客、机器人，或是一个发帖声称教皇支持特朗普的马其顿青少年。这种情况破坏了文明讨论，助长了黑客活动和网络霸凌，也让电子邮件带来了风险。

[H] 互联网先天缺乏安全的身份识别和认证机制，这也使交易变得不便，阻碍了普惠金融，破坏了内容创作者的商业模式，导致垃圾邮件泛滥，还迫使我们使用连逃脱大师胡迪尼都可能被搞糊涂的密码和双因素认证方案。为解决安全问题而投入的巨额资金和计算机人才，使互联网在某些领域拖累了生产力，原本它可以促进生产力。

[I] 在柏拉图的《理想国》中，我们读到古格斯之戒的故事。戴上戒指，你就能隐身，别人也无从知道你的身份。柏拉图问，戴上戒指的人还会讲文明、守道德吗？他认为不会。互联网印证了他的判断。网络已失去作为社群和市场的功能。每天都有更多网站关掉评论区。

[J] 如果可以从头来过，我认为可以这样做。建立一个系统，让内容创作者同内容聚合平台和搜索引擎谈判，使自己的内容每次被使用时都能获得版税，就像美国作曲家、作家与出版商协会为会员作品的公开演出和电台播放争取报酬一样。嵌入简单的数字钱包和货币，方便人们为歌曲、博客、文章及其他出售的数字内容快速进行小额支付。让电子邮件带有经过认证的回复地址或发件地址。尽可能在系统底层保障关键属性和安全，例如在硬件或编程语言中落实这些要求，让安全性由底层提供，免去程序员在每一行代码里单独处理的负担。开发能够更新互联网数据包设计的芯片和机器。有需要的人可以为自己的数据包编码或添加元数据，说明数据包里有什么，以及其中的内容可按什么规则使用。

[K] 多数互联网工程师认为，这些改革在技术上可行，包括 TCP/IP 的共同设计者文特·瑟夫、谷歌的米洛·梅丁，以及麻省理工学院负责网络安全的霍华德·施罗布。施罗布说过：“我们没必要活在网络地狱里。”实施改革主要取决于成本和社会意愿。有些人会抵制任何对匿名性的削减，这可以理解。他们有时把匿名性称为隐私。

[L] 因此，我认为最好的办法是建立一套自愿使用的系统，让愿意使用的人能够验证身份。人们可以自行选择。想匿名交流和上网的人仍然可以这么做。有些时候，我们也会选择表明身份，并只与身份可核实的人打交道，这样做也应当是我们的权利。现实世界正是这样运作的。

[M] 这样做会有许多好处。人们可以更方便、更安全地管理财务和医疗记录。小额支付系统可以让有价值的内容得到回报，改变目前为赚广告费而追逐标题党的激励机制。黑客攻击、垃圾信息、网络霸凌、恶意挑衅和匿名仇恨言论也可能减少，网络讨论有望变得更文明。
